title: What is the difference between flush and commit in JPA/Hibernate? Can data that is flushed but not committed be rolled back?

s1_definition.profdef: A **flush** synchronizes the persistence context with the database by executing the buffered INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements over the open JDBC connection, but it does **not** end the transaction. A **commit** finalizes the transaction: it flushes any remaining changes and then issues the database COMMIT, making all the changes permanent and visible to other transactions. Crucially, changes that are flushed but not yet committed are still inside the transaction and **can be rolled back** — the database holds them in an uncommitted state and will undo them if a rollback occurs.
s1_definition.analogy: Flush is like the teller keying your deposit into the terminal so it appears on their screen and locks the amount in the day's working ledger — but the branch has not yet closed its books. Commit is the branch manager closing the books at end of day, making every entry final and visible to the whole bank. If something goes wrong before the books close, even a keyed-in entry (flushed) can be struck out (rolled back).
s1_definition.oneliner: flush = send SQL to the DB now (still in the transaction); commit = finalize and make permanent; flushed-but-uncommitted changes CAN be rolled back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A **flush** synchronizes the persistence context with the database by executing the buffered INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements over the open JDBC connection, but it does **not** end the transaction. A **commit** finalizes the transaction: it flushes any remaining changes and then issues the database COMMIT, making all the changes permanent and visible to other transactions. Crucially, changes that are flushed but not yet committed are still inside the transaction and **can be rolled back** — the database holds them in an uncommitted state and will undo them if a rollback occurs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Flush is like the teller keying your deposit into the terminal so it appears on their screen and locks the amount in the day's working ledger — but the branch has not yet closed its books. Commit is the branch manager closing the books at end of day, making every entry final and visible to the whole bank. If something goes wrong before the books close, even a keyed-in entry (flushed) can be struck out (rolled back).

**One line to remember:** flush = send SQL to the DB now (still in the transaction); commit = finalize and make permanent; flushed-but-uncommitted changes CAN be rolled back.

sections.s2_technical:
Hibernate buffers changes in the persistence context and uses write-behind. A **flush** is the moment it drains that buffer: it runs dirty checking, orders the statements, and executes them on the JDBC connection. After a flush, the database knows about the changes within the scope of the current transaction, so later statements in the *same* transaction see them, but the transaction has not ended.

```java
account.credit(new BigDecimal("1000"));
em.flush();  // UPDATE accounts SET balance=... runs now, TX still open
```

A **commit** does two things: it triggers a final flush of any remaining buffered changes, and then it issues the SQL COMMIT that ends the transaction and makes everything durable and visible to other connections. In Spring, you rarely call commit yourself — the `@Transactional` proxy commits when the method returns normally and rolls back on a runtime exception.

The rollback point is the heart of the question. Between flush and commit the changes live in an *uncommitted* state inside the transaction. The database isolates them from other transactions (depending on isolation level) and keeps enough information in its undo/WAL logs to reverse them. If a rollback happens — an exception, an explicit `rollback`, or a constraint check deferred to commit — the database undoes even the flushed statements. So a flush is absolutely not a point of no return.

Auto-flush is worth knowing: with the default `FlushMode.AUTO`, Hibernate flushes automatically before executing a query whose results could be affected by pending changes, and always before commit. This keeps queries consistent with in-memory changes. Senior nuances: a flush can acquire row locks and can trigger constraint violations early, so flushing changes *when* errors appear; flushing does not release locks (commit does); and a flush inside a loop followed by clear is the standard batch memory pattern, but each flush is still part of one big transaction that commits or rolls back as a whole.
sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — a transfer debits the sender, flushes, then fails crediting the receiver.** At National Bank of India a money transfer debits Rajesh, and partway through, crediting Priya fails because her account is frozen. Even though the debit UPDATE was already flushed to the database, the whole transfer must undo. This is exactly how flush-then-rollback works — the flushed debit is reversed because the transaction never commits.

**Problem 2 — a mid-transaction balance check must see the just-debited amount.** A fraud rule inside the same transaction queries the balance after the debit and must see the reduced figure. This is exactly why auto-flush runs before the query — so the query reflects the pending debit even though nothing is committed.

What the code will do: a `TransferService` that debits, flushes, runs a fraud check, then credits; if crediting fails it throws, Spring rolls back, and the demo shows both balances restored.

```bash
# Build

# Run

# Attempt a transfer into a frozen account (will roll back)

sections.s5_journey:
Input: transfer 50000 from SAV2001 (Rajesh, 1000000) to CUR3001 (Priya, FROZEN).

Step 1 — both accounts are loaded as managed entities with snapshots.

Step 2 — `rajesh.debit(50000)` changes the in-memory balance to 950000. No SQL yet.

Step 3 — `em.flush()` executes the UPDATE on the sender, so the database now shows 950000 for Rajesh within this transaction. The transaction is still open and nothing is committed.

Step 4 — the fraud-check query runs; auto-flush guarantees it sees the debited 950000, confirming that flushed changes are visible inside the same transaction.

Step 5 — Priya is frozen, so the method throws AccountFrozenException. Spring's transactional proxy catches the runtime exception and rolls back.

Step 6 — the database undoes the flushed debit. Rajesh is back to 1000000 and Priya is unchanged at 250000. The flush was not permanent because commit never happened.

```
2026-10-24 01:13:01 INFO  Debited 50000 from SAV2001; flushed (uncommitted)
2026-10-24 01:13:01 INFO  In-transaction balance for SAV2001 seen as 950000.00
2026-10-24 01:13:01 ERROR Account frozen: CUR3001 → transaction ROLLED BACK
2026-10-24 01:13:01 INFO  SAV2001 restored to 1000000.00 (flush undone)
```

```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Flush vs Commit (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Unit of Work: buffer changes, flush as a batch            │
  │  Proxy (Spring @Transactional): commit/rollback around call│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: service does transfer; TX manager owns commit/rollback │
  │  D: depends on EntityManager + declarative TX, not raw JDBC│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Sequence ──
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ @Transactional begin (TX manager opens JDBC TX)          │
  │   debit() → in-memory change                             │
  │   flush() → SQL executed, NOT committed                  │
  │   query  → auto-flush → sees pending change              │
  │   throw  → TX manager ROLLBACK → undo flushed SQL        │
  │ (normal return → final flush + COMMIT → durable)         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a flushed change ──
  [BUFFERED] ─flush─▶ [IN-DB, UNCOMMITTED] ─commit─▶ [DURABLE]
                                │ rollback
                                ▼
                            [UNDONE]

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. transfer()  2. debit()  3. flush() → UPDATE
  4. fraud query (auto-flush)  5. frozen → throw
  6. Spring rollback → DB undo  (balances restored)

  (Caution) flush ≠ commit. (Caution) flush takes locks but does not release them (commit does).
  Rule: flush makes SQL visible in-TX; only commit makes it permanent.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A flush synchronizes the persistence context with the database by executing the buffered insert, update, and delete statements on the open connection, but it does not end the transaction. A commit does two things: it performs a final flush of anything still buffered and then issues the database commit that makes every change permanent and visible to other transactions. The single most important point for an interview is that changes which are flushed but not yet committed are still inside the transaction and can absolutely be rolled back, because the database keeps them in an uncommitted state with enough undo information to reverse them.

The reason flush exists separately from commit is visibility and timing within the same transaction. With the default auto flush mode, Hibernate flushes automatically before a query whose results could depend on pending changes, and always before commit, so my in-memory changes and my query results stay consistent inside the unit of work. A flush also lets constraint violations and lock contention surface early, at a known line, rather than at commit. But a flush does not release locks and does not make anything durable; only commit does that.

At National Bank of India our transfer service debits the sender, flushes so an in-transaction fraud query sees the reduced balance, and then credits the receiver. In one case the receiver's account was frozen, so after the debit had already been flushed to the database we threw a runtime exception, Spring's transactional proxy rolled the transaction back, and the database undid the flushed debit, leaving both balances exactly as before. That is the proof that a flush is not a point of no return. The nuances I always mention are that in Spring I almost never call commit myself because the Transactional proxy commits on normal return and rolls back on a runtime exception, that a flush acquires row locks it only releases at commit, and that in batch jobs I flush and clear in chunks for memory, but every one of those flushes is still part of one transaction that succeeds or fails as a whole.

---

keyPoints: flush(): push pending SQL to DB — NOT permanent, TX can still rollback
commit(): make changes permanent — cannot undo after commit
flush does not end the transaction — it only synchronizes state
Hibernate auto-flushes: before queries, on TX commit
